title: Machines
tagline: Study simple machines, mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency.

overview.intro: Machines are devices that make work easier by changing the magnitude or direction of effort. This chapter focuses on simple machines such as levers, pulleys and inclined-plane-related systems, introducing mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency. Understanding how machines trade force for distance and how friction affects performance helps in solving numerical problems and interpreting practical applications.

facts.label: Velocity ratio
facts.value: VR = distance moved by effort / distance moved by load

learningOutcomes: Define load, effort, mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency.
Explain the principle of a lever and classes of levers with examples.

Relate gain in speed or force multiplication to machine design.
Solve numerical problems involving simple machines and losses.

learn.title: Basic Terms and Principle of Machines

blocks.text: A machine is a device that allows work to be done more conveniently, for example by applying a smaller effort to overcome a larger load or by changing the direction of force. The load (L) is the resistance overcome by the machine, and the effort (E) is the force applied to it. Machines do not create energy; in an ideal machine, input work equals output work.

Mechanical advantage (MA) is the ratio of load to effort: MA = L/E. Velocity ratio (VR) is the ratio of distance moved by effort to distance moved by load in the same time. Efficiency η is the ratio of useful work output to work input, and for practical machines η = (MA/VR) × 100% is less than 100% due to friction and weight of moving parts.

items: MA can be greater than, equal to, or less than 1 depending on machine type.
VR is determined by geometry and is independent of friction in ideal analysis.
Efficiency is reduced by friction and energy losses.
A machine may provide force gain, speed gain, or direction change.

blocks.text: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum. By applying effort at one point, a load can be moved at another. The principle of levers is based on the principle of moments: in equilibrium, effort × effort arm = load × load arm, giving MA equal to the ratio of effort arm to load arm in an ideal lever.

Levers are classified into three classes based on relative positions of fulcrum (F), load (L) and effort (E). Class I (F between E and L) includes seesaws and crowbars and can provide MA > 1 or < 1. Class II (L between F and E) includes wheelbarrows and nutcrackers and always provides MA > 1. Class III (E between F and L) includes tongs and human forearm and provides MA < 1 but speed/distance gain.

A pulley is a wheel with a grooved rim over which a rope passes. A single fixed pulley has its axis fixed; it changes the direction of effort and has VR = 1 and ideal MA = 1, making lifting more convenient. A single movable pulley has a pulley that moves with the load; in the ideal case it provides MA = 2 and VR = 2, reducing effort required.

Pulley systems such as block and tackle combine fixed and movable pulleys to achieve higher velocity ratios. The VR of a block and tackle system is generally equal to the number of rope segments supporting the load (depending on configuration). Actual MA is less than VR due to friction and weight of pulleys and rope.

items.text: Single fixed pulley: effort 100 N lifts 100 N load (ideal), direction changed.
Single movable pulley (ideal): effort 50 N can lift 100 N load.
items.note: Effort moves twice the distance moved by load.

learn.title: Efficiency, Gain in Force and Gain in Speed

blocks.text: No practical machine is perfectly efficient because some input work is wasted overcoming friction and moving parts. Efficiency expresses how effectively a machine converts input work to useful output. As friction increases, MA decreases for a given VR, lowering efficiency. Lubrication and good design can improve efficiency but cannot eliminate losses entirely.

A machine can be used as a force multiplier when MA > 1, meaning a small effort moves a large load over a smaller distance. It can act as a speed multiplier when MA < 1 and VR < 1 in certain arrangements, where effort moves a short distance to move the load faster or farther. The choice depends on the task, such as lifting heavy loads or increasing speed in tools and body movements.

items.meaning: The resistance or weight overcome by a machine.
The force applied to a machine to do work.
Ratio of distance moved by effort to distance moved by load.

blocks.text: Numerical problems typically require calculating MA from load and effort, VR from distances or pulley arrangement, and efficiency from MA and VR. Units must be consistent, and loads/efforts may be given in newtons or kilogram-force (converted using g if required). Diagrams help identify supporting strands and lever arms correctly.

In an ideal machine, MA = VR and efficiency is 100%. In real machines, MA < VR. When effort moves through a distance, input work is E × dE; useful output is L × dL. Comparing these values provides another way to compute efficiency and understand energy losses.

items: State MA and VR as ratios (no units) unless specified otherwise.
Efficiency is expressed as a percentage.
Count supporting rope segments carefully in pulley systems.
Check whether the machine is ideal or practical before equating MA and VR.

keyPoints: Machines make work easier but do not reduce the total work required in ideal conditions.
Mechanical advantage MA = Load/Effort; velocity ratio VR = effort distance/load distance.
Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100% and is less than 100% for practical machines.
Levers are classified into three classes by positions of fulcrum, load and effort.
Class II levers are force multipliers; Class III levers provide speed/distance gain.
Single fixed pulley changes direction (ideal MA = 1); single movable pulley gives ideal MA = 2.
VR in pulley systems depends on the number of supporting rope segments.
Friction reduces MA and efficiency but not geometric VR.
Correct identification of arms, distances and strands is crucial in calculations.
Units of load and effort must be consistent when computing ratios.
examFocus: Define MA, VR and efficiency and derive the relation η = MA/VR.
Identify lever class from diagrams and state its mechanical advantage characteristics.
Calculate MA, VR and efficiency for lever and pulley systems.
Determine VR of pulley arrangements by counting supporting strands.
Explain why efficiency of practical machines is less than 100%.
Distinguish force multiplier and speed multiplier with examples.
Show clear steps and correct ratios in numerical problems.

questions.prompt: Mechanical advantage of a machine is defined as:
questions.answer: Load/Effort
questions.explanation: MA compares the load overcome to the effort applied.
questions.commonMistake: VR is the ratio of distances, not forces.

questions.prompt: A single fixed pulley (ideal) has a mechanical advantage of:
questions.answer: 1 (unity)
questions.explanation: An ideal single fixed pulley changes direction but does not multiply force.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse fixed pulley with movable pulley.

questions.prompt: A wheelbarrow is an example of a:
questions.answer: Class II lever
questions.explanation: In a wheelbarrow, the load is between the fulcrum (wheel) and the effort (handles).
questions.commonMistake: Identify positions of fulcrum, load and effort carefully.

questions.prompt: Velocity ratio of a machine is given by:
options: distance moved by load/distance moved by effort
distance moved by effort/distance moved by load
questions.answer: distance moved by effort/distance moved by load
questions.explanation: VR compares displacements of effort and load in the same time.
questions.commonMistake: Keep effort distance in the numerator.

questions.prompt: Efficiency of a practical machine is always:
questions.answer: less than 100%
questions.explanation: Friction and other losses prevent all input work from becoming useful output.
questions.commonMistake: An ideal machine has 100% efficiency, but practical machines do not.

questions.prompt: In a Class III lever, the mechanical advantage is usually:
questions.answer: less than 1
questions.explanation: Effort is applied closer to the fulcrum than the load, giving speed/distance gain rather than force gain.
questions.commonMistake: Class II levers, not Class III, are force multipliers.

questions.prompt: If MA = 3 and VR = 4, the efficiency is:
questions.commonMistake: Do not invert the ratio MA/VR.

questions.prompt: A single movable pulley (ideal) has VR equal to:
questions.answer: 2 (twice)
questions.explanation: The effort moves twice the distance of the load in an ideal single movable pulley.
questions.commonMistake: A single fixed pulley has VR 1, not 2.

questions.prompt: The fixed point about which a lever turns is called the ________.
questions.answer: fulcrum
questions.explanation: Fulcrum is the pivot point of a lever.
questions.commonMistake: Load and effort are forces/positions, not the pivot.

questions.prompt: The relation between efficiency, MA and VR is η = ________ × 100%.
questions.answer: MA/VR
questions.explanation: Efficiency is the ratio of mechanical advantage to velocity ratio expressed as a percentage.
questions.commonMistake: Ensure MA is divided by VR, not multiplied the other way.

questions.prompt: In a practical machine, mechanical advantage is ________ than velocity ratio.
questions.answer: less
questions.explanation: Losses due to friction make actual MA smaller than the geometric VR.
questions.commonMistake: They are equal only in an ideal machine.

questions.prompt: Define mechanical advantage and velocity ratio.
questions.answer: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load to effort (MA = L/E). Velocity ratio is the ratio of the distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load in the same time (VR = dE/dL).
questions.explanation: MA involves forces while VR involves distances.
questions.commonMistake: Do not interchange the definitions.

questions.prompt: State one advantage of a single fixed pulley and one advantage of a single movable pulley.
questions.answer: A single fixed pulley changes the direction of effort, making it convenient to lift a load. A single movable pulley provides a mechanical advantage of 2 (ideal), allowing a smaller effort to lift a heavier load.
questions.explanation: Each type offers a different practical benefit.
questions.commonMistake: An ideal fixed pulley does not multiply force.

questions.prompt: A machine lifts a load of 200 N with an effort of 50 N. Calculate its mechanical advantage.
questions.answer: Mechanical advantage MA = Load/Effort = 200/50 = 4.
questions.explanation: MA is a ratio showing how many times the load exceeds the effort.
questions.commonMistake: Keep load in the numerator and effort in the denominator.

questions.prompt: Why is the efficiency of a practical machine less than 100%?
questions.answer: In a practical machine, part of the input work is wasted in overcoming friction between moving parts and in lifting the weight of machine components. Therefore, useful output work is less than input work, making efficiency less than 100%.
questions.explanation: Energy losses prevent complete conversion of input to useful output.
questions.commonMistake: Mention friction as a key cause of reduced efficiency.

questions.prompt: Describe the three classes of levers with the relative positions of fulcrum, load and effort and one example of each.
questions.answer: Class I lever: fulcrum is between effort and load (E–F–L), e.g. a crowbar or seesaw. Class II lever: load is between fulcrum and effort (F–L–E), e.g. a wheelbarrow. Class III lever: effort is between fulcrum and load (F–E–L), e.g. tongs or the human forearm. The class depends on the arrangement, which determines whether the lever multiplies force or provides speed gain.
questions.explanation: Correct ordering of F, L and E defines each lever class.
questions.commonMistake: Use clear examples that match the stated arrangement.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an ideal machine and a practical machine in terms of MA, VR and efficiency.
questions.answer: In an ideal machine, there are no frictional or other losses, so work input equals work output. This means mechanical advantage equals velocity ratio (MA = VR) and efficiency is 100%. In a practical machine, losses occur due to friction and the weight of moving parts, so output work is less than input work. Consequently, MA is less than VR and efficiency is less than 100%. The velocity ratio, being determined by geometry, remains the same for a given machine configuration.
questions.explanation: Losses affect MA and efficiency but not the geometric VR.
questions.commonMistake: Do not state that VR changes due to friction.

questions.prompt: In a block and tackle system with 4 supporting strands, an effort of 150 N lifts a load of 450 N. Calculate MA, VR and efficiency.
questions.answer: Mechanical advantage MA = Load/Effort = 450/150 = 3. Velocity ratio VR = number of supporting strands = 4 (for this system). Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100% = (3/4) × 100% = 75%. Therefore, MA is 3, VR is 4 and efficiency is 75%.
questions.explanation: VR is taken from the pulley arrangement while MA comes from measured forces.
questions.commonMistake: State assumptions if strand counting depends on configuration; use given supporting strands here.

questions.prompt: Why is a Class III lever called a speed multiplier even though its mechanical advantage is less than 1?
questions.answer: In a Class III lever, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load, so the effort arm is shorter than the load arm. This gives MA = effort arm/load arm < 1, meaning effort is greater than load. However, a small movement of the effort produces a larger movement of the load in the same time, increasing speed or distance moved by the load. Hence it acts as a speed or distance multiplier.
questions.explanation: Trading force for distance results in greater load displacement.
questions.commonMistake: Explain both the disadvantage (MA < 1) and the advantage (speed gain).

questions.prompt: A lever has an effort arm of 40 cm and a load arm of 10 cm. Calculate its ideal MA. What effort is needed to lift a 200 N load in the ideal case?
questions.answer: For an ideal lever, MA = effort arm/load arm = 40/10 = 4. Since MA = Load/Effort, Effort = Load/MA = 200/4 = 50 N. Therefore, the ideal mechanical advantage is 4 and the required effort is 50 N.
questions.explanation: Longer effort arm relative to load arm provides force multiplication.
questions.commonMistake: Use consistent length units when forming the ratio.

questions.prompt: A single movable pulley system has an efficiency of 80%. Calculate the effort required to lift a load of 400 N. Comment on how friction affects the effort compared to the ideal case.
questions.answer: For a single movable pulley, VR = 2. Efficiency η = (MA/VR) × 100%, so 80 = (MA/2) × 100, giving MA = 1.6. MA = Load/Effort, hence Effort = Load/MA = 400/1.6 = 250 N. In the ideal case (100% efficiency), MA would be 2 and effort would be 200 N. Friction reduces efficiency and MA, so a greater effort (250 N instead of 200 N) is required to lift the same load.
questions.explanation: Comparing ideal and actual cases shows the effect of energy losses.
questions.commonMistake: Use VR = 2 for a single movable pulley unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: How can the efficiency of a pulley system be improved in practice? Explain why it cannot reach 100%.
questions.answer: Efficiency can be improved by reducing friction through lubrication of axles, using lighter pulleys and smoother ropes, and maintaining proper alignment. However, it cannot reach 100% because some energy is always lost to friction and to moving parts of the system, so work input will always exceed useful work output.
questions.explanation: Practical measures reduce losses but cannot eliminate them completely.
questions.commonMistake: Give realistic improvements and a clear reason for unavoidable losses.
